results.summary: This is the clocking block of a RISC-V scan-chain based CPU. It provides a slow clock output and drives a 7-segment display counter that increments every second after reset. The design is intended to be tested by observing the counter on the display. The documentation is minimal, with a TODO for how it works, so details of the clocking scheme are not described.

This is the instructions block of a RISC-V scan-chain based CPU. It drives a 7-segment display counter that increments every second after reset. The design is intended to be tested by observing the counter on the display. The documentation is minimal, with a TODO for how it works, so details of the instruction handling are not described.

The design is intended to be tested by observing the counter on the display. The documentation is minimal, with a TODO for how it works, so details of the register file are not described.

The design is intended to be tested by observing the counter on the display. The documentation is minimal, with a TODO for how it works, so details of the ALU are not described.

This is a simple FSK modem comparable to Bell 103. It transmits using triangle wave synthesizers and receives by heterodyning, FIR filtering, and phase detection. It is configured over SPI and requires external analog hardware such as a comparator and an R-2R DAC for the phone line interface. The design supports serial data at 300 bps, but the documentation notes that noise immunity is questionable.

This is a small persistence-of-vision display controller. It stores an 8x32 image in memory, which can be updated over SPI, and uses a hall effect sensor to synchronize the display with rotation. It outputs to a line of eight LEDs and requires external hardware including LEDs, an MCU for image loading, and a means of timing. The design generates 48-128 pulses per hall cycle and handles blanking.

This is a 4-bit sequential ALU that takes operands and opcode serially and outputs results with flags. It operates on each clock cycle when enabled and takes an additional cycle to output the result. The design is tested using cocotb and Icarus Verilog, with a Makefile provided for running test suites. It is a straightforward arithmetic unit with no external hardware requirements.

This design implements a ring oscillator with skew correction using a differential clock ring. It includes grey counters to test the stability and frequency of the oscillator, with results displayed on a 7-segment display. The design is controlled by a select input to choose which counter to read, and it outputs a divided clock ratio. The original extended design did not fit in hardware, so only a subset is implemented.

This is a base-10 grey counter that counts from zero to a trillion, changing only one output bit per count. It groups bits into decimal digits and provides various output selections via input pins to view different digits on the 8 outputs. The design is tested with cocotb, and the documentation explains the decoding scheme and potential race conditions. It is a novel take on grey counters with decimal digit grouping.

This is a 4-bit single-cycle CPU with a simple RISC/Accumulator ISA. It includes a register file, ALU, and 7-segment decoder, with instructions and register selections provided via input pins. The design was tested with a ModelSim TCL script and a cocotb testbench is planned. It requires no external hardware and outputs to a 7-segment display.
